notes.meaning: God tells Aaron that he, his sons, and the Levites must carry the burden for any wrongs done against the holy sanctuary. The priests alone were held responsible for mistakes made in their priestly duties. Serving God in leadership brings serious accountability, not a reason to boast.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note a careful chain of liability where priests answered for temple ritual errors, while Levites answered for boundary violations around the sacred tent.

notes.meaning: Aaron is commanded to bring his fellow Levites to assist him and his sons before the Tent of Meeting. The Hebrew name Levi sounds like the word for joined, showing they were partnered with the priests. The Levites served in the outer courtyard, while the priests served at the altar and inside the holy place.

The Levites were assigned to guard and maintain the tent, but they were forbidden to approach the altar or the sacred furnishings. If an assistant touched the sacred objects, both the assistant and the priest who permitted it would die. God set clear boundaries so that holy things were treated with deep reverence.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary emphasizes that the Levites were barred from offering the actual sacrifice and sprinkling blood, which belonged to the priests alone.

notes.meaning: The Levites were appointed to stand guard and handle the general work of the Tent of Meeting alongside the priests. No outsider, meaning anyone from another tribe, was allowed to come near this work. This kept the Lord's dwelling place safe from unauthorized intrusion.

The priests had to carry out their duties at the altar and in the sanctuary with great care. By serving faithfully, they prevented God's holy anger from falling on the nation of Israel again. Faithful ministry shields God's people from harm.

The Lord reminded Aaron that the Levites were chosen from among the people as a gift to him. They were dedicated to the Lord to perform the heavy physical work of the Tent of Meeting. Good helpers in the work of God are a great blessing.

Only Aaron and his sons were allowed to serve at the altar or go behind the inner curtain. God gave them this sacred office as a pure gift of grace, not as something they earned. Any unauthorized person who pushed in to do this work was to be put to death.

God told Aaron that the holy offerings brought by the Israelites were given to the priests for their food. Because the priests were anointed to serve, these gifts belonged to them and their families by a permanent law. God took care of the daily needs of those who served his altar.

The priests received the portions of grain offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings that were not burned on the altar fire. These were most holy gifts and could only be eaten by the male priests inside the Tabernacle courtyard. God provided food for his servants directly from the sacrifices brought to him.

The priests also received special gifts that were lifted up to the Lord, called wave offerings. Unlike the most holy sacrifices, these foods could be eaten at home by both sons and daughters. Anyone in the priest's household who was ceremonially clean—free from ritual defilement—could eat them.

The priests were given the finest fresh olive oil, new wine, and grain presented as firstfruits. The first ripe fruit brought from every harvest belonged to Aaron and his family. Any family member who was ceremonially clean could share in this harvest.

Everything in Israel that was permanently devoted to the Lord was handed over to the priests. This included dedicated property, livestock, or goods that could be used or eaten. What was dedicated fully to God became support for his workers.

The firstborn of every human and animal belonged to the Lord and was given to the priests. Firstborn sons and unclean animals could not be sacrificed, so families had to redeem them, meaning buy them back with money. For a month-old baby boy, the price was set at five silver shekels.

Firstborn cattle, sheep, and goats were holy and could not be bought back with money. Their blood was splashed on the altar, and their fat was burned as an offering pleasing to God. The meat was then given to the priest, just like the breast and right thigh of peace offerings.

God promised all these sacred offerings to Aaron and his descendants as an unbreakable covenant of salt. Salt was used to preserve food, so it became a symbol of a promise that would never spoil or fade away. God's commitment to support his ministers was permanent.

The priests were told they would receive no tribal territory when Israel entered the promised land. Instead, the Lord himself was their portion and their inheritance. Having God as our true treasure is far greater than owning land.

God gave the Levites the tithes—the tenth part of all crops and livestock—as their regular income. This was their pay for the hard work they did serving at the Tent of Meeting. Because they had no farm tracts, the community supported them through God's law.

differ.view: The tithe began before Moses and continues as a lasting moral guide for Christian giving of at least ten percent.
The tithe was part of the old covenant system for Levites, so believers today should give generously and willingly without a fixed ten percent rule.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Church teachers historically saw Christian clergy as successors to the Levites who should be supported by tithes, though compulsory tithing has ceased today.

notes.meaning: Ordinary Israelites were strictly warned never to approach the Tent of Meeting to carry out sacred duties. Stepping into the sacred work of the priests and Levites brought fatal guilt and death. God placed this rule to guard the community from judgment.

The Levites had the duty of guarding the holy tent, and they had to bear the guilt if they were careless. Because their life was set apart for ministry, they received no tribal land in Canaan. Their full attention belonged to the house of God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church fathers such as Cyprian saw the Levites' freedom from land as a model for Christian clergy, who should stay unentangled by worldly business in order to focus on ministry.

notes.meaning: The tithes offered by the Israelites to the Lord were given directly to the Levites as their inheritance. The Levites received this food as God's gift rather than as human charity. This divine provision took the place of farmland.

The Lord told Moses to give instructions to the Levites about their own giving. When the Levites received the tithe from the people, they were required to give a tenth of that tithe back to the Lord. Even those who lived on gifts were expected to give to God.

God promised that the Levites' gift would be counted as real grain from a threshing floor or fresh juice from a winepress. Even though they did not farm land, their gift was fully accepted by the Lord. God honors sincere giving from whatever resources he provides.

The Levites were commanded to take this tenth of the tithe and hand it over to Aaron the priest. This provided food for the high priest and the working priests at the altar. In this way, every level of God's ministers supported the wider worship of the Lord.
The Levites had to give the very best and holiest part of every gift they received. They were not permitted to give leftovers or inferior goods to the Lord. True worship means giving God our best.

Once the Levites had given the best tenth to the priests, the rest of the tithe belonged entirely to them. They and their families could eat it anywhere with a clear conscience. It was their earned compensation for their labor at the Tent of Meeting.

By giving the best portion to the Lord first, the Levites kept themselves safe from guilt. If they kept the best parts for themselves, they would defile the holy offerings and face death. Putting God first protects his servants from spiritual disaster.
